claims.text: As-reported HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
As-reported HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
The reported 13.5% terminal strain for HfZrTiTa0.53 is a tensile fracture strain and can serve as the baseline for uniform tensile elongation.
As-reported HfZrTiTa0.53 is in a high-strength but low-tensile-ductility state.
Cold rolling followed by optimized annealing can induce a dual-phase microstructure containing a homogeneous nanoscale dispersion of ductile precipitates in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Thermomechanical treatment can control precipitate size, morphology, and distribution and thereby optimize strength and ductility in multicomponent alloys.
Fine, uniformly distributed ductile precipitates will produce a more uniform stress distribution in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Fine, uniformly distributed ductile precipitates will mitigate localized crack initiation in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The proposed ductile phase will increase dislocation mobility during tensile loading.
The proposed ductile phase will facilitate crack blunting during tensile loading.
A fine dual-phase or precipitate-containing microstructure can combine high strength with enhanced tensile ductility.
Maintaining load-bearing paths through the primary refractory matrix will preserve the alloy's yield and compressive strengths.
The treatment will increase uniform tensile elongation by at least 20%, from 13.5% to approximately 16.2% or more.
The treated alloy will retain yield and compressive strengths near 786 MPa and 1314 MPa, respectively.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has proven impact-triggered energy-release behavior.
The thermomechanically treated HfZrTiTa0.53 will retain impact-triggered energy release comparable to the untreated alloy.
The tensile and compression predictions are restricted to room temperature and a quasi-static strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
Impact-energy retention is to be evaluated under dynamic conditions comparable to thin-steel-target penetration testing.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is variously treated as terminal strain, tensile fracture strain, and the baseline uniform elongation. Fracture or terminal strain and uniform elongation are distinct measurements, so the asserted change from 13.5% to 16.2% uniform elongation is not internally measurement-consistent.
